performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The Largo of “Winter”, RV 297, from Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons, sets the solo violin by the fire while the orchestral violins play the rain against the window. Vivaldi wrote the raindrops pizzicato and forte, with the bass kept quiet beneath them.

sections.label: A · Solo violin over pizzicato, Largo
sections.mNote: Bowed solo violin above pizzicato violins and bass

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody returns from B♭
sections.mNote: The opening tune returns in B♭ and moves towards E♭.

sections.label: Coda · solo E♭ over pizzicato violins
sections.mNote: The solo violin holds E♭; the pizzicato violins continue.

cues.title: Winter sonnet, letter E
cues.text: “Passar al foco i dì quieti e contenti” (“To spend the days by the fire, peaceful and content.”) The 1725 sonnet moves the scene indoors. The solo violin plays in E♭ major over plucked violin notes, and the bass is marked always quiet.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, letter E; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, II, opening bars, bass marked Sempre Piano: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351. Italian text also at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Four_Seasons_(Vivaldi).
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Pizzicato rain, orchestral violins
cues.text: “Mentre la pioggia fuor bagna ben cento” — “While outside the rain soaks a hundred others.” The orchestral violins play pizzicato throughout. After its first cadence in B♭ major, the solo melody starts again from B♭ and moves back towards E♭.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter E; translation ours. Italian text at https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996; Mutopia score, II, bars 8–16, with La Pioggia and Pizziccati forte in the orchestral violins.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Letter to Guido Bentivoglio, 1737
cues.text: In November 1737 Vivaldi wrote to his patron Guido Bentivoglio that he had not said Mass in twenty-five years. The cause was a chest ailment he had had from birth, his “strettezza di petto”. He was ordained in 1703 and stopped saying Mass after leaving the altar three times before the end of the service.
cues.evidence: Vivaldi to Marchese Guido Bentivoglio, Venice, 16 November 1737, in Karl Heller, Antonio Vivaldi: The Red Priest of Venice (Amadeus Press, 1997), Appendix, letter 5, pp. 287–288: no Mass in twenty-five years, “the ailment from which I have suffered from birth”, three departures from the altar, “constriction of the chest”. Michael Talbot, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, gives the phrase “strettezza di petto” and the ordination in March 1703. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/antonio-vivaldi_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Closing bars, solo E♭
cues.text: The solo violin reaches E♭ and holds it through the last bars. Below, the orchestral violins continue their plucked semiquavers, the rain of the movement. They stop only at the final fermata, where they hold the chord.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 16–18: the solo E♭ is tied across the closing bars, and the orchestral violin semiquavers end at the final fermata: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The melody begins again on B♭
transitions.from: A · Solo violin over pizzicato, Largo
transitions.to: A′ · Opening melody returns from B♭
transitions.how: At the end of the first eight bars the solo’s C trill resolves to B♭. The melody then begins again on B♭, a fourth below its original E♭. The plucked violins and the quiet bass continue underneath, and the altered second half leads back to E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 7–16; the two-phrase design is described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/02.php.

transitions.title: Held solo E♭ over pizzicato arpeggios
transitions.from: A′ · Opening melody returns from B♭
transitions.to: Coda · solo E♭ over pizzicato violins
transitions.how: The solo’s D rises to E♭ and is held. Beneath the held note the orchestral violins continue their pizzicato E♭-major arpeggios until the final fermata.

composer.epithet: Venetian composer of concertos for the women of the Pietà and operas for the city’s theatres, who wrote a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 Antonio Vivaldi, a twenty-five-year-old Venetian, was ordained priest in March and became a violin teacher in September. He had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and went on helping with his career long after the son had become famous. In Venice Antonio was known as il prete rosso, the red priest. He worked in the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year. In 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 they took him back.
